title: Tests that catch bugs
summary: Good tests try the edges: zero, negatives, exactly-on-the-line values and both sides.

title.never: A test that can't fail is useless
title.bit: Tests must be able to fail

say.never: A test only helps if it would **fail** when the code is wrong. That's how this lesson grades you: the checker plants a bug in the code, one at a time, and runs your tests. If all your tests still pass, they missed that bug. Your job is to write tests that catch every one.
say.bit: The checker plants bugs; your tests have to fail on every one of them.

say.never: Most bugs live at the **edges**. Test a normal value, and then: zero, a negative number, a value exactly **on** the line (19, not just 25), and a value on each side of it. One test from the middle passes almost every buggy version.
say.bit: Test a normal value plus zero, negatives, exactly-on-the-line, and both sides.

say.never: Get the expected value from a calculator or from the rules, **not** by running the code and copying what it prints. If the code is wrong, copying its answer just writes the bug into your test.
say.bit: Get expected values from the rules, not from the code's own output.

board.code:
// 3 feet is 36 inches, worked out by hand:
Assertions.assertEquals(36.0, Units.feetToInches(3.0), 0.0001);

steps.title: In your lesson: Bugs hide at the edges

say.never: For `clamp`, try a value below `min`, one above `max`, and one in between. For `inchesToMeters`, 1 inch is 0.0254 m: try a whole number, a value with a fraction like `2.5`, and a negative distance. If a checkpoint names a bug that slipped through, that's a hint about which edge to add.
say.bit: clamp: below, above, inside. inchesToMeters: whole, fraction, negative.
